name: The Hundred Schools and Their Heirs: Thought in Old China
description: Confucius, Mencius, the Taoists and the Legalists argue in a time of war, then an empire chooses among them, and later scholars remake the winners.

checkpoints.name: The age of Confucius
checkpoints.note: Confucius taught that a good society rests on family duty, learning and moral example. Followers collected his sayings in the Analects, and Confucianism grew from them. Sun Tzu is credited with The Art of War, and Classical Chinese became the language of learning.

checkpoints.name: A hundred schools
checkpoints.note: The Warring States period, when rival kingdoms competed, produced rival ideas. Mencius held that people are born with the seeds of goodness, the Mohists urged impartial care for all, Taoists followed the Tao Te Ching, and Legalists argued for strict laws and strong rule.

checkpoints.name: Qin and Han
checkpoints.note: The Qin dynasty united China in 221 BCE. Its first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, used Legalist methods, joined older walls into the Great Wall, and was buried near the Terracotta Army. The Han dynasty that followed gave Confucian learning an honoured place at court.

checkpoints.name: The Song rethinkers
checkpoints.note: Under the Song dynasty scholars rethought Confucian ideas in answer to Buddhism and Taoism, a movement called Neo-Confucianism. Zhu Xi gathered and explained the classic texts, and his commentaries shaped how later generations were taught.

checkpoints.name: Ming and the mind
checkpoints.note: In the Ming dynasty Wang Yangming argued that moral knowledge is within every mind and must be shown in action, a challenge to Zhu Xi's emphasis on studying the principles of things. His teaching spread widely, reaching Japan and Korea.
